mr:0905-ioannes-bonus-de-siponto.note: The monastery of Saint Michael was on the island of Mljet (Meleda, Q211306), as the Italian edition says; the Latin names only the Dalmatian coast facing the Gargano (Q763332). The Pulsano martyrology (Acta Sanctorum, June IV, p. 41) says John of Matera sent John as abbot to the island of "Melita", and a bull of Alexander III of 9 February 1177 lists "ecclesiam sancti Michaelis in Meleta" among the possessions of Pulsano (Q3603280; A. Cavallini, Santa Maria di Pulsano, 2002, p. 178). L. Mattei-Cerasoli (La Congregazione benedettina degli eremiti pulsanesi, 1938, pp. 12, 15) places it opposite the Gargano and rejects Malta (Q233), whose "island of Saint Michael" took that name only in 1555; he has John sent to govern the monastery, where the Martyrology says he built it. Which church on Mljet it was is disputed: the church of Saint Michael near Babino Polje (Q3442639, Sutmiho), the late-antique basilica at Polače (Q3443490), or an earlier shrine on the islet of Saint Mary (Q1454858) in the Great Lake (I. Tomas, Prilozi povijesti umjetnosti u Dalmaciji 43, 2016, pp. 78-79; Institute of Art History, Zagreb, conservation study of Saint Mary on Mljet, 2022).

mr:0927-bonfilius.note: The monastery of Storace was the Benedictine abbey of Santa Maria di Storaco (Q141922767) near Filottrano (Q124029, Ancona). U. Nicolini (Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani 12, 1971) writes that Bonfilius, born at Osimo (Q124554) about 1040, "giovanissimo entrò a S. Maria di Storaco in quel di Filottrano (Ancona), cenobio del quale più tardi sarebbe diventato abate" (entered it very young and later became its abbot). The Comune di Filottrano's history of the site says the abbey was built in the 11th century on a hill north-west of the town, was destroyed with the castle of Storaco around 1200, and was replaced by a shrine of the Virgin; the present church of Santa Maria di Storaco (Q119193681), rebuilt from 1351 around the older apse, stands on the site.

mr:0930-gregorius-illuminator.note: The cave is the Caves of Manē (Manēay ayrk‘) on Mount Sepuh (Q47530516), in the district of Daranali (Daranaghik‘, Q4155003) near Kemah (Q1023301) in the valley of the Western Euphrates (Karasu, Q1728989), Erzincan, Turkey; it lies far upstream of the confluence of the Karasu and the Murat (Q913193), so the Martyrology's "confluence" is loose. Agathangelos (History 4.13) has Gregory found "on the mountain called the Caves of Mane, in the province of Daranalik". Movses Khorenatsi (History of the Armenians II.91, tr. R. Bedrosian) names the mountain after Mani, a companion of Hripsime who lived there "in some caves of the rocks", and says "It was in this cave that the blessed Gregory also resided"; shepherds buried him there unrecognized, and his remains were later found by the ascetic Garnik, "who brought them to the village of T'ordan" (Tortan, Q10756769, the monastery of Surp Pırgiç on the mountain's western slope, a separate site). A. Manoukian (Fundamental Armenology 1 (9), 2019, pp. 170-171) identifies the hermitage with the Avag Monastery, "also known among Armenians as 'Hankist Lousavorch‘i Vank‘' or 'Maneay Cave'", and Armenian Wikipedia places the cave Manēay ayr beside the spring of the Great Illuminator Monastery (Q107324554) on the western slope of Mount Sepuh. The cave's exact position is not mapped.

mr:0107-clerus.note: The 2004 edition commemorates a deacon and martyr of Antioch on 14 January as Glycerius (mr:0114-glycerius-antiochiae) and does not print Clerus, who is probably the same martyr under a corrupted name: the Bibliotheca Sanctorum takes Baronius's “Clerus” for a second entry of Glycerius; the Hieronymian Martyrology gives the name of the Antioch deacon in several forms (one manuscript has a deacon Lucerus at Antioch on 7 January) on 7, 13 and 15 January; and the other names recorded for Clerus (Licerius, Lycerius, Lucerius, Bilicerius) are forms of Glycerius. Not settled: no source states the identification outright or explains the 2004 date, 14 January, which is the day the Syriac Martyrology gives a deacon Glycerius of Nicomedia; and some calendars have Glycerius of Antioch drowned, as the Syriac Martyrology says of another Glycerius at Antioch (8 June), where the historical editions have Clerus beheaded.

mr:0205-genuinus-et-albuinus.note: The 1914 English fuses the eulogies of Ingenuinus and Albuinus of Brixen, which the 1749 edition and the 2004 edition print separately (mr:0205-ingenuinus, mr:0205-albuinus).

mr:0214-valentinus-interamnae.note: The 2004 edition has a single Valentine (on the via Flaminia), generally identified with the bishop of Terni; the 1749 and 1914 editions print both eulogies on this day.

mr:0220-eleutherius-et-socii.note: The 1749 edition names Eleutherius, bishop, and 128 others in Persia on February 20; probably the eulogy of Sadoth, bishop, and 128 companions (mr:0218-sadoth-et-socii): same place, king (Sapor), number and refusal to adore the sun.

mr:0504-triginta-novem-martyres-phaenoni.note: The 1749 and 1914 editions print the thirty-nine martyrs of the mines of Phaeno as a eulogy of their own, after that of Silvanus of Gaza; the 2004 edition commemorates them together with him in mr:0504-silvanus-et-socii.

editions.martyrologium_romanum_1914_en_unofficial: Translation error: 'Lucius' where the Latin has 'Mucii'.

mr:0813-hippolytus.note: The Hippolytus buried in the Ager Veranus is traditionally the Hippolytus of the 2004 eulogy mr:0813-pontianus-et-hippolytus, which leads with Pontian and tells a rewritten narrative.

editions.martyrologium_romanum_1914_en_unofficial: This text is the rewritten eulogy of the Twelve Brothers of Benevento and does not name Donatus or Felix; it succeeds the 1749 eulogy, which mentions the twelve brothers' feast and Benevento, but its subject differs.

mr:0905-quinctius-et-socii.note: The 2004 edition reduces the eulogy to Quintus alone (mr:0905-quintus).

editions.martyrologium_romanum_1914_en_unofficial: This text joins the Octave and the Seven Sorrows in one sentence, with no clean point to split it; the Seven Sorrows half corresponds to mr:0915-maria-perdolens.
Translation error: the 1749 Latin calls him 'Episcopi Abrincensis et Confessoris', not a martyr.

mr:0928-marcus-et-socii.note: The 2004 edition drops Mark and leads with the three brothers.

editions.martyrologium_romanum_1914_en_unofficial: Translation error: the Latin is a translation of relics (Translatio), not a birthday.

mr:1030-maximus-apameae.note: The historical editions place Maximus at Apamea; the 2004 edition places him at Cumae (mr:1030-maximus).
